speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND THE PRESIDENT
speechtext:
That it be resolved by the	[DOT] [DOT][DOT]
House of Commons that it is expedient that parliament do approve of the convention between His Majesty and the President of the United States of America, signed at Washington on the twenty-third day of January, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-four, for the purpose of avoiding any difficulties which might arise between them in connection with the laws in force in the United States, on the subject of alcoholic beverages, a copy of which has been laid before parliament.
That a message be sent to the Senate informing their honours that this House has adopted the above resolution and requesting that their honours will unite with this House in the approval of the above-mention convention.
And that the clerk do carry the said message to the Senate.
He said: Mr. Speaker, very shortly after the opening of parliament, I laid on the Table a copy of a convention between the United Kingdom and the United States of America, respecting the regulation of the liquor traffic. This subject was one of consideration and of discussion at the Imperial Conference last fall. It is referred to in the summary of proceedings of the conference which has also been tabled. I might quote from the reference, to be found on page 12 of the summary, the paragraph that is pertinent. It reads as follows:
During the session of the conference, the question of the regulation of the liquor traffic off the American coasts and of the measures to be taken to avoid a serious conflict either of public opinion or of official action was seriously debated. The conference arrived at the conclusion that, while affirming and safeguarding as a cardinal feature of British policy the principle of the three mile limit, it was yet both desirable and practicable to meet the American request for an extension of the right of search beyond this limit for the above purpose, and negotiations were at once opened with the United States government for the conclusion of an experimental agreement with this object in view.
I should like to give to the House the essential provisions of the convention, or treaty as it may be called, and will do so, in as brief a form as possible:
The principle that three marine miles from low water mark constitute the proper limits of territorial water is upheld.
Appropriate provision is made for the searching of British vessels under stated con-
Prohibition in United States

ditions; and when there is reasonable cause for belief that the vessel has committed or is committing or is attempting to commit an offence against the laws of the United States prohibiting the importation of alcoholic beverages the vessel may be seized and brought into the United States for adjudication.
It is provided that this right of seizure may be exercised within the distance from the coast that may be traversed in one hour by the vessel suspected of endeavouring to commit the offence. Where a transfer from one vessel to another is contemplated, it is the speed of the latter vessel which is to determine the distance from the coast within which seizure may be made.
The treaty also provides that no penalty or forfeiture under' the laws of the United States shall attach to the carriage of alcoholic liquors by British vessels when listed as sea stores or as cargo destined for a port foreign to the United States, provided that such liquors are kept under seal continuously while the vessel is within the territorial waters and that they shall not at any time or place be unladen within United States territory. Such carriage is to have the same status as now provided by law with respect to the transit of alcoholic liquors through the Panama canal. Provision is made for reference to a joint commission of claims for compensation where a British vessel has suffered loss or injury through any unreasonable or improper exercise of the rights conferred by the treaty. The treaty is subject to ratification in the usual manner, and is to remain in force for one year from the date of the exchange of ratifications. Three months before the expiration of the year modifications may be suggested by j either party, and if no agreement is made with respect to them the treaty is to lapse; otherwise it is to continue from year to year subject to a similar right of proposed modifications. The treaty is also to lapse if either of the parties is prevented by judicial decision or legislative action from giving full effect to its provisions, and in case from any cause the treaty comes to an end, such party is to enjoy all the rights he would have possessed had it not been concluded.
The convention was signed at Washington on January 23 of this year by the British ambassador, Sir Auckland Geddes, representing His Majesty the King, and by the Hon. Mr. Hughes, Secretary of State of the United States, representing the President. It has since been ratified by the Senate of the United States on March 13, by a vote of 61 to 7.
It will be ratified by the King as soon as approval of the treaty has been given by the

parliament of the United Kingdom and the parliaments of the several self-governing dominions. On January 12 of this year the Canadian government was asked if its ministers approved of the terms of the treaty, and also if they were agreeable to having the British ambassador sign the treaty. On the day following a reply was sent to the British government intimating that the terms of the treaty were agreeable to our ministers; also that the government was agreeable to having the British ambassador sign. The reply drew attention to the particular clause in the treaty which refers to vessels which may be illegally seized and brought into port. We fell, that if the vessel seized should happen to be under Canadian registry it was but right that the British representative on the board appointed to adjudicate upon the matter should be a person nominated by the Canadian government ; we also felt that the government should only give its approval subject to the subsequent approval of this parliament. These two intimations were given in our despatch, and in the reply which was received from the British government it was intimated that the wish of Canada in both those particulars would be fully respected.
I will, for purposes of greater accuracy, indicate to the House more or less in the language of the despatch itself, the form in which our approval as a government was given to the terms of the treaty. The despatch, sent on January 12 intimated-that: The government of Canada, subject to acquiescence by the British government in the conditions therein mentioned, approved of the proposed treaty with the United States, and approved of the signature of the treaty by His Majesty's representative at Washington. It had been decided that parliamentary approval should be obtained before concurrence in ratification should be intimated. It was stated that the Canadian parliament would probably meet before the end of February. That the Canadian government's present approval of the proposed treaty was given on condition that it was understood that if a joint board to report upon the claims of compensation by a vessel of Canadian registry is required to be constituted under Article 4, the selection of the person whose name is to be submitted to his Majesty for appointment to the board will be made by it. In conclusion the despatch said it was assumed that an undertaking by the British government on this point would be sufficient and that provision with reference thereto need not therefore be included in the treaty.
The reply sent stated that it was quite understood that the Canadian government

Prohibition in United States
would wish to obtain the approval of the Canadian parliament before ratification, and that a similar course was contemplated in the United Kingdom; that his Majesty's government would readily leave to the Canadian government the nomination of the person to be the member of the joint board referred to in Article 4 in respect of vessels of Canadian registry and agreed that it was not necessary to make provision in the treaty, further that the same procedure was contemplated in case of other dominions.
As I have intimated, the treaty was signed on January 23rd by the British ambassador. In this connection may I point out to the House that the practice followed with respect to the signature of this treaty is the one decided upon at the recent Imperial Conference and set out in the report of the Summary of Proceedings of the Imperial Conference to be found on pages 13, 14 and 15 in the part of the report relating to negotiation, signature and ratification of treaties. With reference to the signature of treaties there are the following provisions:
(a)	Bilateral treaties imposing obligations on one part of the Empire only should be signed by the representative of the government of that part.
The Halibut treaty which has been the subject of discussion in this House is of that character. It is a bilateral treaty which imposed obligations only on Canada, not on other parts of the British Empire, and as such according to the procedure which the Imperial Conference has thought proper in this matter, it should be signed by a representative of the government of Canada. Now I continue to quote from the report of the proceedings:
The full power issued to such representatives should indicate the part of the Empire in respect of which the obligations are to be undertaken, and the preamble and text of the treaty should be so worded as to make its scope clear.
(b)	Where the bilateral treaty imposes obligations on more than one part of the Empire the treaty should be signed by one or more plenipotentiaries on behalf of all the governments concerned.
This treaty between His Majesty and the President of the United States is a bilateral treaty which imposes obligations on more than one part of the Empire. It imposes obligations on all parts, and therefore it is, in the language of the procedure set forth by the *conference, to be signed by one or more plenipotentiaries on behalf of the governments concerned. It would seem quite sufficient that the British Ambassador should be sole plenipotentiary for this purpose. I might say I am informed that the governments of Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Newfoundland, and the Irish Free State have all approved of the terms of the treaty, and have all expressed their acquiescence in having the British Ambassador sign the treaty in so far as their interest in the matter is concerned. The act of ratification is an act of the sovereign. The treaty while it has been ratified by the United States has not yet been ratified by His Majesty the King. That ratification awaits, as I 'have already intimated the concurrence of the governments of the several parts of the Empire before that step is taken.
In regard to the ratification of a treaty, the Imperial Conference has the following to say with respect to procedure:
Ratification of treaties imposing obligations on more than one part of the Empire is effected after consultation between the governments of those parts of the Empire concerned. It is for each government to decide whether parliamentary approval or legislation is required before a desire for or a concurrence in ratification is mtimated by the government.
It will be seen by the statement I have just read that it is not essential to ratification that parliament should approve treaties. Ratification being an executive act may be taken by the executive independent of parliament altogether, should the executive of the country, in other words the government concerned, so desire. We have felt that in these important' matters of treaty the parliament should be asked to approve before the government would concur in the ratification. It is with a view of obtaining the approval of the parliament of Canada that to-day we are asking this House to pass the resolution which I have just presented. In recommending the adoption of the resolution, I do so on the grounds which have been urged in the United Kingdom and elsewhere, namely: First of all, there is the ground of morality, that it is obviously desirable for countries to unite in endeavouring to give effect to the laws of other friendly countries, particularly where those laws have in view serving a great moral purpose. There is next, and closely allied, the ground of international good-will. There	is reason	to believe that	the
United States is most anxious that this course should be taken; that this treaty should be passed, and we in Canada, as a near neighbour, will I think, feel gratified at an opportunity of being able to facilitate in any manner possible the furtherance of friendly relations between Great Britain and other parts of the British Empire and the United States. By giving our approval in a whole-hearted manner to this treaty, I think we shall be helping to serve that end. Finally, it has been represented by British shipping interests that it will be very much to their

advantage that this treaty should be enacted. While, on the one hand, it gives to the United States government the privilege of the right of search beyond the three-mile limit to a point which, roundly speaking, it has been estimated might be set at somewhere within the vicinity of twelve miles, with a view of assisting the United States government to enforce its legislation restricting the importation of alcoholic beverages, on the other hand, it gives to British shipping interests the right to carry alcoholic beverages under seal into United States ports, provided that those alcoholic beverages are kept under seal when within the three-mile limit. On these grounds, therefore, of commercial interest, moral obligation and international good-will, I recommend the adoption of the resolution by the House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONVENTION BETWEEN HIS MAJESTY AND THE PRESIDENT
speechtext:
With regard
to the first question which my right hon. friend has asked: How is it ascertained that a bilateral treaty applies to one particular part of the Empire or more than one, I would answer that that fact would be ascertained by the terms of the treaty itself, its subject matter and by conference between the different parts of the Empire. The paragraph in the report of the Imperial Conference which deals with the subject of negotiation of treaties, contains, I think, what will answer 
my right hon. friend's question. The paragraph reads:
(a)	It is desirable that no treaty should be negotiated by any of the governments of the Empire without due consideration of its possible effect on other parts of the Empire, or, if circumstances so demand, on the Empire as a whole.
(b)	Before negotiations are opened with the intention of concluding a treaty, steps should be taken to ensure that any of the other governments of the Empire likely to be interested are informed, so that, if any such government considers that its interests would be affected, it may have an opportunity of expressing its views, or, when its interests are immediately involved, of participating in the negotiations.
If that course is pursued, I think it will soon become apparent ro any particular selfgoverning dominion or the government of the United Kingdom, whether the treaty which it proposes to negotiate is one that concerns only one part of the Empire or more than one paH. In these, as in all matters, common sense has to govern in the last degree; hard and fast lines cannot be laid down; but the broad intelligence that is usually applied to matters of this sort would soon, I think make it quite apparent and clear whether a sell-governing dominion or the government of the United Kingdom would be justified in regarding a treaty as imposing obligations only upon itself.
As to the second question which my right hon. friend has asked

on whose advice does His Majesty act in ratifying a treaty, was it?

speechtext: No, in a case, for example, of a treaty which, after the conference, the other dominions and the United Kingdom should agree affected Canada alone. In this report of the Imperial Conference is mention of the legal adviser of the Foreign Office, who was present when the particular matter to which my right hon. friend refers was discussed at a subsidiary conference. His name is Sir C. J. B. Hurst. Perhaps I can best illustrate the point of view which was expressed at that time, by recalling, as best I can at the moment, an answer made by Sir Cecil Hurst to a question that was asked by one of the dominion prime ministers. It was in the nature of a rhetorical reply. In the event of advice being given to His Majesty which might prove to be not proper advice, and the necessity should arise for impeaching the minister or prime minister who had given it, would it, asked Sir Cecil, be the British Prime Minister or the

Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs of Great Britain, or the minister or prime minister of the dominion concerned against whom impeachment proceedings should be properly started? That question was put in that way to elucidate where the responsibility began and where it ended. I gathered, I think rightly, that the interpretation which the Foreign Office placed upon the matter to which my right hon. friend just referred is this, that the government of the Dominion which was tendering the advice in such a case was the government that was responsible; that it was advising His Majesty direct in regard to matters which were of sole concern to the dominion; that in the transmission of that advice the British government was acting as the channel through which that advice was transmitted, but was not the government which was formally tendering the advice.

hon. friend will see that these are all matters of constitutional development. Up to the present time all communications have gone to His Majesty through the British government. It will also be seen that it is obviously desirable to have some central agency or channel through which'

I think it would be palpably unwise to have different parts of the British Empire communicating direct with His Majesty, without any knowledge on the part of other parts of the Empire that such advice was being given in that way. I consider it advisable that in the working out of a great constitutional evolution-for that is really what is involved in these matters steps should be taken slowly and with great caution.

Mr. Speaker, although undoubtedly under this treaty the right of Great Britain to send British vessels into American ports with liquor has been finally admitted by the United States, it should never have v been necessary to have such admission, as Great Britain undoubtedly always had that right. In addition to the apparent omission which the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Baxter) has called to the attention of the government, I would mention another Canadian problem which I think might very well have been discussed and settled in connection with this treaty. It concerns the province of British Columbia and the Yukon territory. Because of the geographical situation it is impossible to send anything into the northern part of that province and the Yukon territory except through Alaska. Now, the United States in the interpretation of its prohibition law holds that it is illegal to send liquor across any portion of the United States. In British Columbia and in the Yukon territory liquor is handled solely by the government. Up till 1922 no objection was raised by the United States authorities to the importation of liquor across Alaska for the use of northern British Columbia and the Yukon, but early in that year they announced that no further importation would be permitted. I understand negotiations have taken place between the government of Canada, on behalf of the government of the Yukon territory, and the government of the United States, but that as yet our neighbours are unwilling to concede us-shall I say this privilege? I prefer to call it our right-they are indisposed to revert to the former practice, although tine liquor is sent up the coast in Canadian vessels in bond, unloaded into railway cars at the dock and within a period of two hours transported across
United States territory in bond into Canadian territory. Consequently we are prevented from receiving any further importations there. The attitude of the United States, to my mind, is nothing more nor less than that of the dog in the manger; they will not themselves have liquor in Alaska, and they will not let us have it in the Yukon.
There has been no illicit traffic in liquor from Yukon to Alaska. As a matter of fact the government of the Yukon territory imports only such a moderate quantity as, after careful calculation, they are assured is sufficient to meet the reasonable needs of their population. I submit the same question as that put by the hon. member for St. John in the language of the United States: What do we get out of this? That is the question the United States' asks on every occasion, international or otherwise. I submit there is not enough in this treaty for us, and if by holding up its ratification the government can bring about a restitution of the right of importation by the government of British Columbia across Alaska into the I ukon territory, most certainly this course should be taken. It is a very important matter for the people of that part of Canada. The governments of British Columbia and the Yukon derive quite a large revenue from their control of liquor. There is no intemperance because the government importations are, as I have already stated, strictly limited to local needs, so that naturally there is an absolutely temperate use of liquor. In the old days saloons were just as numerous there as in other parts of the Dominion, but under the present system the use of liquor is not abused.
The action of the United States in this matter is decidedly unfriendly and absolutely unnecessary, and could be reversed quite easily if they wish to convenience us. Although, I understand, correspondence is now proceeding between the government of Canada and the government of the United States in relation to renewal of our right to import liquor across Alaska for government purposes yet the earlier correspondence extending over the past two years has been entirely without avail, and I submit that once this treaty is ratified and the United States get what they want, Canada will never secure what she is entitled to. I would therefore urge that the government should take into consideration this very serious problem of the Yukon territory and northern British Columbia and withhold consent to the treaty until the United States changes its attitude in the matter.

pleting this tower, we should well consider another part of this item, No. 139, which is now before the committee, namely the expenditure of one and a quarter million dollars or more for a building in London. If there '.s to be any postponement for purposes of economy, that is the item that should be postponed rather than the tower, although at tha. same time good reasons might be shown why the tower also could wait for one, two or perhaps three years. I should, however, like to see the tower completed within some reasonable 'time.

I should like to bring
this to the minister's attention in supporting, in a measure, what my hon. friend has just said. Let us grant for the moment the desirability of completing the tower as regards external appearances. I hurriedly took down a few items, not all by any means, which the minister mentioned of what might be called more or less luxuries in connection with the tower. Someone suggests the term "frills." I do not want to cast any aspersions upon this splendid building, but certain things are not altogether necessary, for instance, reflector lights for windows, $27,000. I appreciate that it is very nice to have these windows beautifully illuminated, but at present $27,000 seems to me a large sum to expend on that particular class of work. There is an item of $16,000 for copper roofing. That is, I take it, merely for the tower. Perhaps that might be necessary if the tower were gone on with, although a less expensive roofing might do for the time being. I do not, however, press that point. Then there is an item for elevators in the tower. I know it is going to be very nice in years to come to provide an elevator in the tower for tourists and sightseers to go up this splendid tower and to have the view. I believe about $30,000 is put in for that purpose. That is an item that could very well stand. We have an item for electric light fixtures through the building. I think hon. members will agree that we are pretty well satisfied for the time being with the light fixtures through this building.
What does my hon. friend mean by "for the time being"?

Perhaps for the next five years. At least let the existing fixtures wear out their life of usefulness. It will be necessary, in any case, before very long to replace a certain portion of them. If they are more
or less temporary, they certainly are not very objectionable to the eye; they are not offensive to anyone. Let them remain as they are for a while so that we shall get the full value of their temporary nature, and then put in your permanent fixtures. For that I think $50,000 is put in, a very large sum. There is an item for certain fancy grill work, 810,000. That might very properly be left for a few years. We have been putting up this building for about eight years; the government has brought the building to a fairly good stage of completion and I think there is quite a bit of national pride in the building, which pride I believe, is justified. I have mentioned items -and I have missed some-totalling about $140,000 that might very well stand over for one, two, three, four or five years. Perhaps no particular harm would be done if these items stood over for four or five years. A moment ago the minister mentioned some equipment and I presume he referred to the equipment in a building next to the Connaught building. I am not aware of the exact conditions of the contract; but if I recall it correctly, it is a cost plus contract. If we do not go on with the work, we do not pay for it. If the work stands, there is no outlay, no demurrage, no penalty on the government for delay. I do not think the contractors would lose or suffer anything or be unjustly dealt with if nothing were proceeded with. I will not, however, press that point. The hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) has brought it forward, I think, properly, and it is desirable that it should be considered. Assuming, however, that we go on with the tower, would it not be quite sufficient to finish the substantial portion of it, that is the stone work and the brick lining-the masonry-without finishing the fancy wrork in the interior- elevators, electric light fixtures, grill work and so forth? I would suggest that the minister review the estimate and delete from it those extras, at least, and ask the House for simply a sum necessary to complete the tower as regards external appearance. There are some other suggestions I wish to make regarding the other items before the whole resolution passes, but I should like to have the minister's opinion on this point first.

The advisability of going on with the tower was given careful consideration, and after the whole situation was reviewed, it was concluded that it would be better for us to continue the work and complete the tower. As regards the electric wiring, anyone accustomed to building knows that that class of work should go on during the time
Supply-Public Works

of construction. It can be properly done then. As regards the elevators, the government has already made a large expenditure on elevators, and this is an additional sum. As to lighting the tower, I do not think anyone would say that we should refrain from expending a certain sum of money which must be expended if we do not want the tower to remain dark. If we put up the tower, it should surely have a light, and the clocks, when they are put in, should be properly lighted. These things are all necessary; they can be better done now than at a later period, and I think we should go on with them. I am not very particular about the carving and electric fixtures in the building; but we have a very fine building with fine corridors, and many people from all parts of the world visit this parliament the year round. It is quite proper that in such a place of interest, a building the beauty of which people visit the Capital to admire, we should have things as nearly as possible in perfect harmony. We have succeeded in cutting this estimate down quite appreciably and I can assure the House that it is not the intention of the government to enter upon extravagant expenditures; but as regards these fixtures I think it is only right that from time to time we should get them installed until gradually we have the whole building completed.
Does the estimate provide this year for all electrical fixtures?
No.

I dislike wearying the House with my economic notions, but there are a few words which I desire to say in addition to the plea that I have made that this unnecessary work be not proceeded with. First of all, it is absolutely unnecessary. There is no more reason for proceeding with the work this year than there was last year, and we were able to d scharge our legislative duties perfectly and in comfort then without this tower. I want to submit these reasons in the hope that the government will be brought to see the matter in the same light as I do. We have a demand from the taxpayers of the country, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, that economy shall be the first order of the day. The government-and I give them credit for it.-have courageously started cutting down; they have cut down the Civil Service in Ottawa. Under these circumstances I would ask them to consider the feelings of some poor man who has lost his position in the Civil Service, who is unable to find other employment and is walking 
the streets of Ottawa, and who would see this tower being erect'd knowing that it is a work that is absolutely unnecessary, however beautiful it may be. So far as the embellishment of the building is concerned, I think the whole strucim e is beautiful as it stands, and if it is to be embellished it must receive the very best works of art. These works of art will be acquired as the years go by, and we ought to see to it that they are the very best that can be obtained. If we get such works, we shall of course have to pay for them accordingly. While the min-' ister was speaking, and particularly when he stated that one expenditure must inevitably lead to another, I could not help thinking of the young couple who were almost ruined because, at the time of their marriage, some rich relation gave *hem a beautiful mantel clock. A rug had to be bought to be in keeping with the clock, something else had to be obtained to be in keeping with the rug, and so on, until finally they had the whole house furnished on a socle very much higher than they could afford I really believe that the government would be meeting the views not only of the vast majority of the members of this House but of the vast majority of the taxpayers if they would abandon the idea of putting up the tower to tne height originally intended. After all, it is not as if the building were an ugly one as it stands. I would remind the minister oc that beautiful building in Paris, Notre Dame cathedral, on which there are two short towers; it is a question among architects whether it was intended to have them built higher or not. The tower on this building undoubtedly is not as beautiful now as t will be when completed, but it is not by any means unsightly; and I cannot imagine many works which would so cast discredit upon the bona fides of the government and their attempt to economise as the continuance of this unnecessary work.

I remember that some
years ago criticism was levelled at the then Conservative government for the extravagance with which it was charged in connection with the problem of putting up this new parliament building. I am glad to be able to say that I was one of those who did not criticise the government of that day for the building they proposed erecting on Parliament Hill, and to-day I shall be amongst those who will have no criticism whatever to offer if the present government endeavour in every legitimate way to make this building

Supply-Public Works
a citadel worthy of the Canadian people. I am surprised that a gentleman of the robust Canadianism of the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) should criticise the government at this stage for attempting to place on Parliament Hill such a building as we ought to have here. My hon. friend declares that it would be extravagant to continue this work, and he says that the government should stand for stringent economy. He tells us that in five years' time we might proceed with the work.
I did not mention any specific date.

The hon. member did not, that is right; but some other hon gentleman on the other side made the suggestion. Well, I think that in five years' time it will be just as extravagant as it is now to complete the building, and perhaps more so.
There might be a more economical government in power then.
I daresay when the Progressives get into power we shall have a more economical government than we have had in either of the old parties.
Just as there was in Ontario.

At least that is what they tell us; and of course you cannot challenge the words of gentlemen in parliament. Now, what does the Minister of Public Works propose? He proposes to do exactly what the people of the country proposed in the first instance when Canada was in the throes of war. We were not afraid then to expend millions in erecting a building on Parliament Hill in which the representatives of the Canadian people should deliberate; and if we had no qualms about spending so much money on this building at a time when the fate of the British Empire was in the balance I do not see any reason for compunction now, when, as I think, there is some measure of confidence on the part of the people as to the future of the country. It is only fitting, I think, that we should have something better than the barn which my hon. friend from Brome would like to see us assemble in.
Oh, oh.

The mere fact that we may be comfortable should not be the only consideration. When parliament met in the Museum the hon. member was no doubt comfortable. But, as a sturdy Canadian, would 36
he be satisfied to see a building on Parliament Hill of the kind which we had in London for so long? Would he have us meet in a building of the sort that has been a public disgrace to Canada for half a century? The hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woods-worth) spoke yesterday about Canadian nationhood. Well, if hon. gentlemen have aspirations in that direction let them see to it that we shall have a building in the capital city worthy of the Canadian nation. I know that we are passing through strenuous times, and there are various ways of retrenching; but from my point of view it would be a mistaken economy to retrench in the way suggested in this instance. Millions of United States citizens visit Washington to see the Capitol and the many other architectural features which go to make it the most beautiful city in the Union. And I, for one, Mr. Chairman, stand for making Ottawa the most beautiful city in the. Dominion.

Mr. Chairman, I quite agree with some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) in regard to economy. With respect to what the last speaker (Mr. Carroll) has said, I doubt if a sense of the practical nature of things always lessens appreciation of the beautiful. I am sure there is many a farmer working between the handles of a plow who enjoys the beauties of the sunset just as thoroughly as some artists who pride themselves on their artistic perception. I admire this building, but I would inform hon. members that in Winnipeg, there is a legislative building of still greater architectural beauty. The members recline on cushioned chairs in the utmost comfort, while the time of the legislature is wasted by lengthy speeches. But there are not many people in the province of Manitoba who to-day feel very well satisfied with that building.
It was not built by the Farmer government, either.
Three-quarters.

It was responsible for about three-quarters of the building.

They were very much in the same position as this government-they had to complete what had already been undertaken by a former government. I do not think we can find fault with the appearance of this building, but we shall be in a better position to deal with the vote after we have received

some further information from the Minister of Public Works (Mr. King). For instance, which would be the more economical course,- to leave the building as it is for a few years or to complete it at once? If I understand correctly, the architect is under a contract to finish the tower, and the contractor is under a somewhat similar obligation. The tower is a very important part of this structure, and it is something that the architect should be held responsible for the completion of. For example, the addition of the final third to its height might develop some latent weakness in the foundations, and therefore it is important that the man who designed the tower should be the man to finish it. Will he be available five years hence? The contractor has a large plant in the city, and I understand the government are paying him a certain sum to hold it here for future use.
No.

If the machinery is removed and the architect not available five years from now, can the work be done as economically as if it were undertaken to-day? I should like some more information from the minister in this connection before I commit myself, because I sympathize with what was said by my hon. friend from Brome. At the same time I want to be practical, I want to know whether it would be a waste of money to defer completion for four or five years. I agree with him that there is nothing unsightly about this building. While the addition of the upper part of the tower might result in greater symmetry the structure is one of which we are all proud. I would rather that we did not spend any more money at the present time, but if I am convinced that it would not be economical to postpone completion for five years, I would say, "Go on and do at least what must be done now, but leave undone anything the postponement of which would not hurt in the long run." I do not know whether the minister can give us any more information that will help us in arriving at a decision on this point.

As I stated before, the government canvassed the situation very carefully, and, as is evident to all hon. members, we have been trying to economize wherever possible. Our technical advisers tell us that it will be more economical to finish the tower now and do the other work I have outlined. We have an arrangement with the architects to complete the designs for the tower. We have also an undertaking with the contractors in regard to their plant now on the ground; it is in these terms:
(Mr. Forke.]
They to furnish the necessary plant for the purpose of such erection without further compensation, provided the plant is held for this work not longer than December 31, 1924. Should it be held later than that date, the contractors are to receive compensation foi the use thereof.
We might cut the estimate now, but in the end I think it will cost us more to complete the work, and certainly the delay will not help the building. I am of opinion that we should proceed and complete the external appearance at least and the electrical wiring, which is part of the early construction and should be installed.

What is the value of the
plant?

The contractors'
estimate is $80,000.
Is that for the whole building?
I understand that is the value of the portion of the plant required to complete this part of the building. A portion of the original plant has been removed.
I suppose it is also a portion of the original plant used in the construction of the main building?
Yes.

Is there any liability to the
contractors or architects under the present contract? I understand the contract requires that the machinery shall remain until the 31st December of this year. Supposing the work is not proceeded with are the contractors entitled to anything? Because, if so, that might be a reason for going on with the work now. I notice about the building many smooth face stones; are these to be cut?
Only a comparatively small portion.
What is the liability?

They have
arranged to keep the plant on the ground up to the 31st December next. More as to any liability I could not say.

Last year the amount of
the vote under this head was $700,000, and this year's appropriation is a revote of $320,000. Can the minister tell us what was done with the $380,000 that was spent last year?

of claim, $253,217.79; coal, $1,497.61; freight on stone from battlefields, $10,378.26; memorial to late Colonel Baker, $9,974.08; sundries, $11,549.31; total $368,379.76.

One would be led by the
estimates to believe that the money had been spent on the construction of this building. What was the nature of the claim settled by the government in the amount of $253,000 odd?

That was by
way of commission paid to the contractors. In the original contract there was a limitation as to the fee to be paid to the contractors as a percentage and also the fee on the total amount. In the case of the architect, after the expenditure had exceeded $5,000,000 *-the limit which had been placed-and was growing larger, the Parliamentary committee in charge of the construction of the building reviewed the situation and made further payments in addition to those due on the $5,000,000 expenditure. In 1921 the architect was demanding more money from the committee, and on the defeat of the late government he resigned, or walked off the job, saying that he could not continue unless he was paid more money. A committee of this House, not appointed by the House but consisting of representative members, conferred with the Minister of Public Works and with the technical officers; the whole situation was reviewed; and it was decided that owing to the alteration in the plans, the extra cost of construction, the changes that followed rapidly after 1916-17, these people were entitled to a reasonable fee. Accordingly a settlement was made and they were paid. The amount of $253,000 was a payment of extra commission earned by the Lyall contracting firm.
What about the architect?
The architect was not paid out of this amount. He was paid out of the 1922-3 appropriation.

What has
been the total expenditure on this building up to date, and what was the original estimate?
The total cost to date has been about $11,000,000. The original estimate was $5,000,000.

Were plans submitted
on which that estimate was based, and if so who was responsible for the changing of the plans to provide for a building that would cost $11,000,000 instead of $5,000,000?

The architect submitted sketch plans to the minister and to the
m
committee and gave his estimate, I believe, as to the cost. It was supposed that there would be a limitation of $5,000,000 upon which the fees of the architect should be applied, but the architect refused to sign the contract as regards the limitation of fees, and he was allowed to continue and did continue with the construction without a signed contract as to the limitation.
Was there not a signed contract as to the amount of his fees?

Yes, the amount of his fees was agreed upon but not signed for in the contract. When we dealt with this matter last year a substantial reduction was made in respect of the amount upon which the architect was to be paid fees;
5 p.m. I think $1,600,000 odd was deducted. The total commission paid to the architect, on the estimate we had last year when the settlement was made, was between four and five per cent, Which, all will understand, is a very low commission for work of this character. The contractors' commissions were on a different basis. For the first $4,000,000 they were paid eight per cent and on the other $1,000,000 they were paid seven per cent. In our settlement with them we made a substantial reduction from the total cost and paid them seven per cent on the balance.
The minister did not give the full terms of the contract. Did the commission not extend to a certain maximum, and not beyond?
I have said that.
I did not hear the minister say it.
I said the architect refused to sign the contract as to that limitation, but was allowed to continue as architect and to construct these buildings.

Will the minister say
whether the contractors are satisfied with this payment of $203,000, and whether that relieves the government of all responsibility up to the present date?
They have released all claims.

I have a recollection that when this item was before the House last year I supported the completion of the tower. It seems to me that when it comes to the question of completing a building like this, in which we have eleven million dollars or more invested, it would be a most unfortunate thing that it
Supply-Public Works

should remain an eyesore for five or six more years when the completion of the building now would add very greatly to its appearance. While I say that, I do not want for a moment to be taken as supporting many of the items which appear in this item of $600,000; for some are of such a character they may well stand. At the same time in constructing a tower such as this it goes without saying that other works such as the installation of elevators, putting in conduits for wiring, and so on, to be done economically must be done at this time. Then there is the further point: If the country is to be liable to the contractor or the architect if the work is not proceeded with this year that is perhaps a further reason why the tower should be completed. I presume if the machinery is taken away now it will cost more to bring it back again and complete the structure at a later period. Therefore I want, so far as I have anything to say, to support the exterior completion of the tower, and the completion of all parts of the structure which are more or less essential such as the wiring and so on, having in mind the promotion of economy. I should like very much if the minister could give us an idea of what portion of the $600,000 would be required for the external completion of the tower, and all such portions which should be finished while the external part is under construction.
Is it estimated that this $600,000 will actually complete the tower?

It will not require $600,000 for the completion of the tower alone. The estimated cost is: Memorial chamber $81,820, and the tower itself $293,808. Then there is the roofing which I think is essential.
The roofing of the tower?

Yes. In this connection there is the copper roof, dormer windows, slate louvres, and so on. I think that will have to be done. Then there are the elevator, enclosures, spiral and straight stairs, and door leading into the tower. These are essential if the work is to be properly attended to. After the tower is completed elevators are necessary. You have nothing to gain by not putting them in when you are at it. The electric wiring, I think, is also essential. This will bring the total to $383,898 for the tower. Adding the other items to which I have referred will bring the amount up to $465,718. As to the height of the tower the present height is 152 feet, and there will be an addition of 128 feet making the. total height 280 feet.

The necessity for going on with this work at the present time, having regard to the need for greater economy, has hardly been proven. Three attempts have been made to secure from the minister some definite statement as to the directions in which economy can be effected but without result. Neither he nor any other member of the House can definitely state that it would be more economical to build now than five years hence. We have in power a government that is pledged to economy. If it is going to reduce the cost of living in the country, possibly it may be more economical to complete this work five years from now than at present. I am delighted to support the position taken by the hon. member for Brome; I think he is on solid ground. With all due respect to my hon. friend (Mr. Boys) I do not think this building in its present state is an eyesore. I think it is a magnificent structure and possibly will be even more magnificent when completed. But at the present time, when the government is discharging many hundreds of civil servants, as one hon. gentleman has pointed out, it is going to be a greater eyesore to these people to see this building completed than to leave it uncompleted. I intend to vote against the item.

I have listened carefully to the discussion and I do not find that a case has been made out to warrant the completion of the tower just now. I do not see that there is any urgency for the completion, or that anything will be lost by waiting. It does not seem to me to be an eyesore. While there will of course be an improvement when the building is completed, conditions are not such as to justify us in proceeding with the work at the present time. When one considers the great buildings of the world there is nothing commoner than to find that years and years are occupied in their completion. It is the commonest experience in connection with the great cathedrals of Europe that the towers are not finished until long periods have passed. The precedents of the past are all in favour of taking adequate time to complete a building of this character. I hope the minister will allow this matter to stand for further consideration.

As I view this question
I think it is about time Canada took a step forward, and there is nothing that will give the country greater confidence than action on the part of the government in a matter like this. It is certainly time the government completed this tower; the uncompleted

Supply-Public Works
state of the tower has been, an eyesore ever since I came to parliament. I think the government is using good judgment in undertaking its completion; it is time the work was carried out.

One aspect of the question has not been mentioned, and that is that the tower is intended to be a memorial to the men who lost their lives in the Great War. There is to be placed in the tower a memorial chamber in which will be recorded the name of every man and woman who served overseas. I believe the architect has received from the government of Belgium and also from the French government, the stone which is to go into that chamber; it comes from the fields of Flanders. Other stone has been received, I understand, from the British government. The material has been brought to Canada, and the governments of these countries have been thanked for their gifts. It is understood this stone is to form part of this memorial. The architect, Mr. Pearson, who has the matter in hand, feels it is imperative that if this work is to be completed it should be done soon. Mr. Pearson, himself as the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) has intimated, is not a young man; he has given his life to this work; he is anxious to see it completed. The government has considered the question of economy most carefully. I think no one who has looked at the estimates which have been presented to parliament and which show a difference of over $46,000,000 contrasted with the total estimates for last year, will fail to realize that if there had been any other direction in which economy could have been practised the government would have followed it.
We have been trying to save all along the line. We talked with the architect and with the technical officers, as the Minister of Public Works has intimated. It was pointed out to us that these contracts were in existence, that keeping the materials stored, keeping the plant stored, and possibly having to reacquaint all the parties who were interested in the work of construction, would involve longer time and greater expense in the end. Consequently we thought it would be mistaken economy not to complete the tower, to say nothing of the memorial feature which I have just mentioned and which the government regards as an important one.
There have been suggestions about placing in the tower a carillon of bells. Anything of that sort which it seemed possible to postpone
we have postponed. Putting in an elevator has been mentioned this afternoon as something which was not necessary during the process of construction, and that it could be put in at any time. The reason this work appears to be necessary is that if it is not done while the work of construction is in process, some part of the work will have to be torn down when such things are put in later on. We have an obligation to the future as well as to the present, and I submit, as the hon. member for Yale-Cariboo (Mr. McBride) has just stated, that it is somewhat of a reflection upon the faith we have in the future of this Dominion, that all over this world the parliament buildings of Canada should be advertised as an incomplete structure. I think that national pride may be appropriately spoken of in this matter, and that the people of Canada would like to see their parliament buildings-so far at least as their external appearance is concerned

in the final form in which it is hoped they will be for centuries to come.

With all due deference to the experience of the hon. minister who has just spoken, I think the greatest memorial we can offer the people is to make Canada a better place to live in. I believe this is a time for essentials. I believe the viewpoint of the people back home, or out in the country, should be considered. I do not believe that viewpoint is favourable to expenditure that is unnecessary at the present time. I think the .finest example we can show this country is to begin the economy right here where it touches ourselves, and I believe the people outside will accept this as true economy. There are some things that are very good for the country, such as the deep waterways, but which are not always expedient. There are some things that may be good if we had the money, but are not very feasible at the present time, and I believe this is one of them. People outside of this House are not only doing away with extravagance, but are even passing up the essentials of life because of the necessity due to present conditions; and I believe this House would give a good lead to the country if it would postpone this matter, and I therefore move that this item of $600,000,, as far as it relates to the building *of the tower, be struck out.

As there is a motion
slightly different from the original motion before the committee, I wish to speak to it. It is a little difficult to undertake to discuss all these things in one item. I am not well enough acquainted with the facts to discuss
Supply-Public Works

the London building, or to say whether it should be there or should not be there; but I have some ideas with regard to the tower that are quite clear. I gather from what the minister (Mr. King, Kootenay) has said that there will be practically no deterioration if it is allowed to rest for a while before being completed. From the peddle who are corresponding with roe I have had more urgent requests for economy than in regard to any other matter. I have not had one request from any community asking that money be expended in that community for any such purposes as the completion of this tower. There are to my knowledge a great many places where people are in sore need of the completion of railways, and that is a matter that would go a long way towards keeping people in our country, so that they might earn something to help build this tower. It is not my wish to make it hard for this government or any other government, but it is a matter of considering where it is best to put our money, because we have not enough to do all we want to do. And, that being the case, I will ask the government to seriously consider the matter before they go ahead with the completion of this tower. I have been asked to press for rural mail routes, and people are applying for mail service a long way from the railways and the centres. I have always been told that the government were not supplying mail routes, and could not do it because they did not have the funds. I hope I will be pardoned for bringing up such matters as this in comparison with the question of the completion of the tower, if it is a sin for me to do it. But the people in the West, in many new localities are pleading for economy, and the privilege of living and making a home in that country. We are spending money to bring people into the country, and we db not want these people to see people going away when they are coming in.

If this amendment
carries it seems to me that it will be a case of false economy. We are all agreed that we should practise the greatest economy possible. We had an example of that fact the other day in the reduction made in the Civil Service bonus and in the reductions also made in the Civil Service. Both of these facts I deeply regret and will discuss them at their proper times. But notwithstanding that it seems to me that the postponement of the building of this tower is a serious mistake. Leaving this beautiful building in an unfinished state seems to show a lack of faith in the future of our country. It is all very 
well to go slowly but we have been going altogether too slowly in completing these buildings. For three years they have been in this uncompleted condition and it is time that the memorial chamber in the tower whioh will be considered as Canada's tribute to our war heroes should be completed.
To my mind the reasons given by the Minister of Public Works are sound, namely that there will be a considerable cost in depreciation to the tower and to the machinery but more particularly because the architect who planned the building should be the one to supervise the final work.

The Prime Minister has advanced the only reason that I have heard given that would influence me to support this appropriation, namely, that it is in the nature of a memorial to those who gave their lives in the Great War. But, on reflection, I recall that the official memorial to those who fell is being erected in France and, I think, this year. Personally, I should like to have seen the main memorial erected in Canada. I have seen the plans for the memorial in France; they are magnificent; but if the main memorial had been erected in the vicinity of the parliament buildings, if we have room, and models of it were erected in positions in France and Belgium, that would have been much more appropriate from the point of view of the country. The idea of this tower being a memorial is splendid; I endorse it; but I draw to the attention of hon. members the fact that the Hall of Fame is likewise part of this memorial, and we have made a start. The sentiment exists; we look upon it as a memorial; I for one am quite content to wait, and I feel I voice the sentiments of the majority of the returned men in this country when I say that as regards the completion of this tower as a memorial, the returned men would be content to wait. The hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride) remarked that it is time that this country showed some confidence and took hold and made a start. I likewise endorse that sentiment; I think it is time that we showed confidence in ourselves; but if this building is only a start, where are we going to end?-we have made a pretty fair start. The start that I suggest and that will create confidence in this country to a greater extent than any other start that we can make as members of this House, is to show the people of Canada that we are really sincere in our desire to retrench. The only way in which we can bring that home is to stop spending. A vital principle is involved in this vote in that it is the first

Supply-Public Works
vote coming before this House, and the time is now ripe to put ourselves on record if we are really determined to carry out this policy of retrenchment. Furthermore, following the minister's reasons for completing the tower, 1 am afraid I cannot agree with the soundness of those reasons. He says that it is more economical to go on with the work now. The only reason advanced for that is the fact that some plant and equipment are tied up to the value of $80,000. I think if we wait we shall probably save $80,000 in years to come in cost of construction. Let us remember that that plant and equipment are the remainder of the plant and equipment used in the construction of the entire building, not specially brought here for the purpose of erecting the tower, and any depreciation of that will be infinitesimal as compared with the capital cost that the country is facing in completing the tower. Therefore, I do not think there is any force in that reason. That is the only liability the country is under to the contractor.
Who let the contract for this building?	.

I do not care who let the contract for the building. I am not concerned with that. Do not think for one moment that I do not .want to see this building completed. I am heart and soul with the idea of completing this building. All that I am suggesting is that there should be a temporary delay in spending any money that we are not absolutely compelled to spend. The reason was advanced that we have the architect with us now. I hope we shall have him with us in the future; but if unfortunately we do not have him with us in the future, we have his plans. His plans do not go with him, and any other architect can follow those plans. The contractors of to-morrow will, we hope, be better than the contractors of to-day, and we shall get just as much efficiency out of the contractors to-morrow in completing this tower as we shall to-day. Consequently, I do not think it is of vital importance that the contractors who are building this on a cost plus basis should be the contractors who will complete the tower.
I was very much interested in the remarks of the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke), and I am interested in knowing where he stands on this and every other item of expenditure that comes before this House. Is he going to carry out this contract with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and support every item that comes before the House, or is he going to carry out his pledge to the people of Canada to effect economy?
I will make it plain how I am going to vote before the vote is taken.

Two alternatives are open: First that any unnecessary expenditures should be eliminated this year; second to support the government because they have introduced this estimate. I hope and trust that the leader of the Progressive party is with the majority in this House, who whether they vote with the hon. member who moved this amendment or not, in their hearts I am sure are with him. We are therefore all very much interested in knowing where the leader of the Progressive party stands on the point.

I have much pleasure in protesting against the amendment, for the simple reason that it will be false economy to leave this tower as it is at the present time. The appropriation is for $600,000. Of that, $320,000 was voted last year and not spent, so that, in other words, we are asking for only $280,000. I am a firm believer that any money that can be spent in this country in an economical way should be spent. It will give an impetus to our country by letting people know that we are advancing. Last night an item was brought up in connection with the colonial building in England to cost $1,250,000, and $750,000, for additions or repairs. When that item comes up again, I will voice my protest against spending that money, because all that we can do by spending that $2,000,000 is to save rent. We could spend that $2,000,000 in Ottawa and save rent, and it would give employment to our own workmen in Canada. I shall have much pleasure when the time comes in voting against the amendment.

I have great pleasure
in associating myself with other hon. gentlemen in the House who have pleaded that the time has not come for false economy. This building in Ottawa does not belong to the city of Ottawa alone, and it is not purely and .simply a parochial sentiment that causes me to rise at this moment, though I am very happy indeed, with my senior colleague, (Mr. McGiverin) to be fortunate enough to represent in this House the capital city of the Dominion. These parliament buildings symbolize the aspirations of the Canadian people, and all that is best in Canadian life, and I take it that hon. gentlemen who sit across the floor having been sent down here to represent the ideals of their constituents, must feel that they owe a duty to them and therefore to the Dominion at large to see that the construction of this monument wherein those ideals are to be given
Supply-Public Works

expression to be completed. For some years the tower has remained unfinished. It has been my privilege to enter daily for two years the Hall of Fame and I have met there every day tourists from all parts of the world, who in no unmistakable terms have expressed their admiration of this beautiful building, but who could not refrain from observing that it is a pity, and indeed a shame, that an appropriate tower has not yet been completed to crown the building. During the summer, streams of water flowed through the front of the hall, and masons have been engaged in cleaning and cutting the stone to remove the marks that have been left by the water that has drained through the tower. No doubt at this moment the country feels the need of retrenchment more than it ever did before. But it seems to me that the Canadian people would have no objection whatever to the completion of this monumental building wherein the deliberations of this young nation take place. I do not think that anyone, be he in humble circumstances or be he affluent, will seriously object that the work be carried out to completion. My colleague and I have to meet the cry for economy, and very stringent reductions have been made, for instance, in the bonus. I do not agree with those reductions. Dismissals are taking place to-day, and with those I disagree. The time will come when I shall have an opportunity of expressing in this House my views on these subjects. But at the present time, although we all feel the pinch of economy-our own constituents do. and I think the same is true all over the Dominion-I also do think it is advisable that the tower be completed so that we may have a fitting building for the parliament of Canada to meet in, and one worthy of the ideals of this Dominion.

T have endeavoured
two or three times, Mr. Chairman, to catch your eye, but being small I am not easily discerned. I asked the minister some questions which he did net answer, one of them being, whether the estimate of five million dollars for the parliament buildings was based on plans that were completed at the time the contract was entered into.

I said no; the
plans were not completed; they were only sketch plans.

Is it possible that the government of a country could enter into an arrangement for the erection of a building of this kind without a definite plan before them? If so, I do not wonder that the work has cost more than double the original estimate.
. 
It is of course futile to lock the door after the horse is gone, but I think the method adopted in the letting of the contract for this building was absolutely wrong. The contract was let on a cost plus basis both to the architect and to the contractor. Obviously, therefore, their whole object was to make every part of the construction as costly as possible in relation to the amount of labour expended; and they leaped a larger reward by building extravagantly than they would otherwise have done. If they built a wall, say, that Was worth only $1,000 and they spent $2,000 upon it, they doubled their reward. That is a principle that is entirely indefensible. Expert ongineere, I understand, were employed to decide hew much of the old walls might safely be retained, and if my memory serves me correctly they reported that there were walls that were safe and sound to the valu;. of some $2,000,000. It might have been more than that, but I think I am safe in slating that figure. As hon. gentlemen know, a committee was appointed by the House to superintend the construction of the work; but I am safe in saying that that committee never functioned as a building committee, and the first thing they knew was that this $2,000,000 worth of walls had been torn down by the contractor without reference to themselves. The contractor got the cost plus for tearing down the $2,000,000 worth of walls although those walls had been declared to be fit for incorporation in the new building. And they also got cost plus for erecting the $2,000,000 worth of new walls that replaced what they had torn down. That made $4,000,000 that was expended at the outset, and they were only where they started at the commencement. There was S per cent paid to the contractor on that $4,000,000, for doing what he should never have done, and 4 per cent paid on the same sum to the architect.
My hon. friend is wrong. He has given the $2,000,000 twice, but they were not paid $2,000,000 for pulling the wall down, but only on the cost of pulling it down.

I accept the minister's correction; I was wrong in that regard. However, I should like to have the information as to what it did cost to pull the old walls down. Now, one of the reasons advanced for proceeding with the construction is consideration for the architect. If I remember rightly, about a year ago, or possibly before that, this same architect held up the completion of the building because the government would not accede to his

Supply-Public Works
terras for what he had already done. I do not think, therefore that we need worry much about the architect and his feelings in the matter. If I am wrong in regard to any of these points I desire to be corrected as I go along. Another matter to which I would refer is the saving that would be derived from postponing the work. I think the minister should seriously consider accepting the amendment of the hon. member for East Peterborough (Mr. Brethen). Let me show what might be saved if the work were postponed. If we did not proceed with it we should save the $600,000 which would otherwise be spent; and there would be a saving of at least 5 per cent, in the way of interest on that money. Someone behind me suggests 6 per cent., but I am putting it conservatively because I do not want to convey any impression of exaggeration. At 5 per cent., that would mean a saving of $30,000 a year in interest; and if the completion of the tower were postponed for a period of five years we should have a total saving in that time of $150,000. As a matter of fact, it would be more than that, because in all probability we should have to raise the money to pay the interest the first years and the interest would therefore be compounded. Possibly in the five years the amount that might be saved would run to about $175,000. It has been stated that the plant to be retained here is worth $80,000. So if we had to replace it new at the end of five years we would still be $100,000 ahead. I do not think any member believes for a moment that the plant to erect a $400,000 structure would cost $80,000. I imagine all of the $80,000 worth of plant would not be needed in the completion of the tower, and I do not suppose such is contended for a moment. I think the minister stated that there were no plans prepared when construction was entered upon. I should like to know just what the undertaking was. Was an architect turned loose by the government of the day to proceed with the construction of a building, without receiving any instructions from parliament or the government as to its dimensions, architectural features and cost? Did somebody just make a random guess that such a building might be erected for $5,000,000?

I might again review the early history of the construction of this building. In 1916 the old building was burned down. The government of the day decided on reconstruction and arrangements were entered into with Mr. Pearson and Mr. Marchand, two eminent Canadian architects, to submit plans to a joint committee of both Houses. Sketched plans were submitted showing the character of the building, with an
estimate based thereon as to the total cost. They suggested that $5,000,000 would be the cost.

Were those the same
plans which were used later on for the construction of a $5,000,000 building?

I will come to
that. The sketched plans originally submitted showed the type and character of the building at an estimated cost of $5,000,000. The plans and estimate were apparently accepted by the committee, and the work proceeded. From time to time changes were made in the plans, with the concurrence of the committee, indeed with the concurrence of parliament, because the vote for the building was discussed each and every year in this House, and as changes were made naturally they involved increased cost. In addition to that, it is not necessary for me to remind the committee, there was a gradual increase in building costs from 1916 onward, and this also accounted for a very considerable portion of the excess over and above the original estimate. I am rather surprised that those who are really anxious to practise economy now suggest that after we have expended some $11,000,000, we are to leave the building uncompleted for the sake of an additional $600,000.
No, we are only urging a postponement of the expenditure.

You are going to
delay completion of the job for five or six years. There is no occasion for this. Besides, every delay so far has cost the people of Canada very considerable sums of money.

Will the minister tell
us in dollars and cents what it would cost approximately to postpone this work?

It is impossible
to furnish such an estimate; it would depend on conditions five years from now, and no one can tell what they will be then. I am informed by our technical advisers that it is better to proceed with the completion of the building now, and that each delay in the past has meant extravagance and increased expenditure. I am satisfied that if this building had been proceeded with right along without delay many thousands of dollars would have been saved to the country.

I want to express my
gratitude and appreciation of the attitude of the minister in answering the aspersions of the hon. member for Victoria and Carleton (Mr. Caldwell). I have observed many a time that when a subject comes up as respects which
Supply-Public Works

there is an attitude of fairness on the part of the Liberal party to the right of the chair, there always arise among those ultra-Grits to my left hon. members who cannot possibly lose an opportunity-which they only imagine exists-of casting some slur, arising wholly out of the basest and most ignorant of partisan prejudice, against the late administration in the construction of this magnificent building. What the minister says as to the plan adopted is precisely correct. The Public Works department could not possibly disrobe itself of responsibility with respect to the construction, but it did disrobe itself of every possible attribute that could be considered partisan, and parliament on the recommendation of the government placed in the hands of a committee of this House and the Senate, composed of members from both parties, all questions connected with the selection of architects, the .adoption of plans, and the method of construction, whether on a cost plus basis or by contract. Everything connected with the undertaking was disposed of and decided by that committee, without any qualification, without any exception. All this I think has been known to ordinarily informed members of this House for many years.
It is true a difficulty arose, having to do with the question of whether a portion of the old building could be used or not. I remember that for some time the committee felt it would be an economy, and wise, to utilize a considerable portion of the old structure. But subsequently they decided otherwise. The wisdom of their decision time has vindicated, and more than vindicated, and I am sure hon. gentlemen by the score can be found on either side of the House to affirm what I now say. It is true-I speak now from memory alone and subject to correction, that one member of the committee, who, I think, was not present at the time the decision was arrived at, afterwards took exception to the course pursued and resigned, but Liberal members of the committee, more thqn one, were present and affirmed the conduct of the committee and stood by the committee to the last. And now their judgment has proven to be correct. I do not think anyone to-day would seriously argue that that portion of the building could have been used, and I do not think anyone would like to have his argument remembered against him in the future who would suggest that $2,000,000 was wasted by not using the old walls, and $2,000,000 more thrown away because they were torn down. The whole history of the structure is a history

honourable to Canada in every way. This is the most magnificent edifice in the Dominion, and in respect of the entire enterprise, from its inception to the present day, there has not been a breath of aspiration as to the honesty of the whole execution.

Will the right hon.
gentleman allow me a question?
I hope it is better than his speech.

Will the right hon.
gentleman deny that two competent engineers have stated that $2,000,000 worth of the old walls were structurally sound and could have been built upon?
I do not deny it, but I know they have been found to be wrong.

By the committee and
by the majority of engineers.

I should like you to
prove that.
You can get an engineer, as you can get a member of parliament apparently, if you are careful enough in your selection, to say almost anything.
Were not those engineers selected by the government of which you *were a member?

Quite so, but there is a
difference of opinion there as elsewhere. But we now know, we are not now engaged in any speculation. We know which was right and which was wrong; experience has proven it.
Were those two engineers discharged, or were they retained until the completion of the building?

As I have already explained, arrangements have been made for completion this year. In fact, the drawings are already being made and within a few days after this item is passed the contractor will be cutting stone, if he is not already doing so. Now, let us just look over this whole situation again.
