Ottawa parliament building, $600,000.

Just before six
o'clock I was going to make a further statement regarding this expenditure. I am rather surprised at the attitude of some hon. members as to the expenditure this year. The government did not originate this expenditure, it was necessitated by a fire which destroyed the parliament buildings. The government of that day saw fit to undertake this obligation and, I think, properly so; the work of -reconstruction was concurred in and agreed to I believe by all. At the end of the year 1921 when there was a disagreement the architect retired. After his retirement the present government came into power, and had certain adjustments to make. Those adjustments have been carried out properly and fairly, I think, and to the satisfaction of all members of this House. In 1922 this parliament voted sufficient money to complete the tower and to finish these buildings. During 1923 it was the feeling of parliament that this work should be done. That being the case, and such having been the attitude of parliament during those two years when adjustments were being made between the government and the architect, and the contractors, the government naturally assumed that they could come before parliament this year and ask for a reduced vote, an amount not as large as the vote of last year. We asked $700,000 last year. We have cut down the expenditure, and we come to parliament and ask for $600,000 now, in order that we may complete the undertaking of the late government and the people of Canada. It has been suggested by the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark) that he will oppose this expenditure and he suggested that $80,000 worth of machinery was a mere bagatelle. Well, it means that if that machinery goes out of the buildings, and if five years from now the government of the day have to enter into a new contract, they will not get a contractor to put the machinery in those buildings and do the work for seven per cent. The architects are eminent in their profession, and I think it is desirable that they should continue the work; and as far as I am personally concerned, as Minister of Public Works, I have gone a long way in order that the construction of this building might be continued, and that those men might complete the construction. I think it is only reasonable and fair, and in the interests of this construction, that those who designed and carried on the work should have an opportunity of completing the building. We have an arrangement with the architects whereby they will design and construct oi supervise the construction of this tower at five and a half per cent commission. When we came to deal with Mr. Pearson last year, after we closed out the old arrangement with
Supply-Public Works

him, did Mr. Pearson offer to do it for five and a half per cent? He said: "No, ten per cent, and fifteen per cent on some features."
There are other architects.

We insisted that the architect should cany it on at five and a half per cent. If this work is not continued at the present time, and if it becomes necessary for the government-I do not say this government, but any government-to enter into a contract at this time for this work, you would not get it done for five and a half per cent, because that is not in accordance with the architectural fees charged in this country. In addition to the plant that is already there and will be available for the completion of this project until December of this year, the government, in the original expenditure, constructed very large sheds or workshops in order that they might satisfy the requirements during a period of four years, because it was intended that this building should be completed in that time. It is now nearly eight years since this work was undertaken, and I am advised that an examination last year of the foundations of these workshops, which cost a considerable sum of money, shows that if we had started the machinery in those shops there would probably have been a catastrophe. They have been deteriorating during the last five years,, and if 3rou leave them there for five years more they will be an eyesore, and you will have to renew them, or spend a large sum of money to put them in shape for this work. Is it desirable for the people of Canada or the members of this House that we should have this hill littered with construction material for five years? Is it the desire of the members of this House that we should destroy the organization built up for the construction of the buildings and delay the work for five years? I think not. I think, in the interests of economy, in view of the fact that this parliament has on two occasions voted money for this work, that it should not be stalled at this time, and that we should proceed with the construction of the tower, the electrical equipment, the installation of elevators, and do the things necessary to complete the work.
I do not believe it would be wise, in fact I think it is absolutely unwise, that we should delay at this time. It is very easy for one to say "The construction of this tower means nothing to me or to my constituents. It is better for me to ask for something for my constituents." But we are dealing with a matter that is national, and I am satisfied that my constituents in British Columbia have suffi-

cient pride in the central parliament buildings .of Canada to desire that that tower shall b? constructed, and to take the advice of the men who were employed, in whom we have confidence, and complete the construction this year.

What is the estimate for
brick and stonework on the tower?

The amount is $383,898. That would be for the Memorial tower and the Main tower. I am satisfied that if hon. members will give this matter a little more consideration they will change their attitude on this question, and I am hoping that the hon. member who moved the amendment that we should not construct the tower but should reduce our estimate by that amount, will see fit to withdraw that amendment, and accept the appropriation. I am satisfied it will be absolutely false economy for us not to continue at this time. If it is left over it will cost a good deal more in the end and we will have the disadvantage of having an uncompleted building in the Dominion of Canada, and this building is one of the first buildings, surely, that should be completed. If our hon. friends would go down to Sussex street to-morrow morning and see that shop, then come up to Parliament Hill and look at the lumbered-up condition there, and then say that they desire to have that remain in its present condition for five years,- that we should stop construction, and at the end of five years build new workshops and bring in new machinery, get a new contract and a new architect-then, so far as I am concerned I do not agree with that, and I think it would be a great mistake.

Might I bring to the hon. minister's attention the suggestion I made before recess? I cannot see for the life of me how you are going to construct or install your elevators this year in any case. I do not think it is physically possible. Why vote some $30,000 for that? Then there is no possibility of installing that very fine and elaborate electrical plant, the reflector, for which $27,000 is to be voted. Why bother about that this year? As I said before, in so far as the lighting system in the building where it is not finished is concerned, I remember looking over some of it at dinner time and it struck me that it was at least not repulsive; and while we would like to see everything finished up in tiptop shape, and all the carving and so forth finished -and I notice the minister provided a very substantial sum for carving-yet these are things that could wait for a while. I would suggest the minister could very well do with

Supply-Public Works
$400,000 at the outside, and have ample to save his investment in equipment and machinery, which seems to be impressing him very much, finish the masonry work on the tower and leave the extras for another year, in view of the fact that very little of it, if any, can be finished during this year. One reason why this appeals to me as reasonable is this-and there are other items in the resolution in the same position-that the government has been making veiy considerable capital, shall I say, out of the reductions in the Civil Service. For instance, as near as I can see, there are about three or four hundred thousand dollars' worth of reductions in the Civil Service in Ottawa. Here we are providing for an expenditure of at least $200,000, in this one item, which apparently is unnecessary and almost impossible to use this year. At the same time we are reducing the staff in Ottawa and discharging employees. I am not complaining about that for a moment; but there is something in connection with this that offends one's sense of justice and decency, and I would suggest to the minister that he drop from the item these extra charges and costs and reduce it to the bare necessity for finishing the masonry work.

As regards the
electrical wiring and the elevator, I think those who have knowledgs of building will agree with me that wiring should be done during the period of construction.

The conduits, but not
the finished reflectors.

The elevator was bought for this tower prior to 1921-2 it is now in the basement or in storage, and it is not being improved but is deteriorating by being there. I think that installation should go on. I think the lighting or the arrangements for lighting should go on. I do not think there should be large expenditures in carving, and that is not intended at all. Last year parliament voted $700,000. We have not carved those stones; we did not expend that money. I think there is certain work that should be done at certain points in this building in order that we may get the benefit ot the expenditure that has been made. Parliament during two years in succession passed this vote when we were not able to go on because we had certain matters to settle, and personally I was not prepared to go on until they were settled and this thing was cleared up. This thing has been cleared up; we are prepared to go on, and I think we should proceed. I am not desirous of having any great carving done; I am satisfied as regards the lighting, but I think we should proceed, and
we shall have to proceed gradually in order to take care of this building and bring it into the position into which it was intended to be brought. I do not think the opposition to this appropriation can be serious because, after all it must be the desire of every Canadian that this building should be completed and not left as it is to-day. I would appeal to hon. members to reconsider the matter and to let us have the money necssary to complete the tower and to do what we find it is economical to do in the matter of wiring, elevators, lights and such things.

When the minister speaks
of the item of $700,000 which was voted last year, it may be that we are right in our conclusion that the government had not the same vision of the need for economy as they have this year and as is expressed by the smaller amount of money asked for. Yet, I must confess, when I read this item, I received the first shock to my sensibilities, in that it seemed to prove to me that the minister or perhaps even the deputy, had not yet fully felt the real need for economy which obtains and has obtained throughout this country for many years now. After leaving the chamber last year and spending about seven months amongst the people who are everlastingly approaching their representatives to demand economy, I find this thought arising in my mind quite naturally: If I could lay this item before the 30,000 odd people who live in my district and ask them what they would do with it. I am quite sure, contrary to the sentiment expressed by the minister to-day, they would say: "Leave it alone; you do not need it at the present time; look at the hundreds, yes, thousands of things left in abeyance in this country longer than the completion of this tower". That is the way in which they would look at the matter. I do not agree with the attitude taken by the minister that we are going to lose so much money because plant, construction machinery, is left here. It seems to me that Peter Lyall & Company are having quite a nice time in receiving from this government certain sums of money for the protection of their implements here and there. I notice in the next item, No. 140, another item where money is to be paid to Peter Lyall & Company for expenses incurred in protection of works during a shut down. Therefore, possibly we may not pay so much attention to this amount of money which is going to be lost in taking care of those implements.
I can quite well understand the attitude of hon. members who represent this city. Naturally enough, as representatives of Ottawa, they would like to see the tower completed;
Supply-Public Works

but, perhaps, their interest and influence might better be exerted, if the money has to be expended, in trying to have the federal area here commenced. In my opinion, in this city, that is a need far greater than the completion of the tower. If the money has to be expended, why not take the full 1600,000 and commence a federal area, so that we can have consolidation and co-ordination of our offices throughout the city? I am sincerely of the opinion that we should practise economy, and this item, the first item we have discussed, brings us to the point that we feel like opposing it. I should like the minister to take the initiative in this and, at least, to reduce the item by a considerable amount.

Perhaps hon. gentlemen are magnifying some of the details. I think the minister would have no objection to letting the item stand until he could look further into the particular items that are mentioned. There is, however, one particular aspect that we must not forget. There was a war a few years ago largely because one party to a contract did not keep it. In the present case there were certain difficulties, as every member, but particularly the Minister of Public Works (Mr. King) knows, that had to be settled with both the contractor and the architect. This House voted money two years ago for the purpose of finishing this tower, the minister in the meantime endeavouring to settle these difficulties, because the prospect of settlement was the only weapon the minister had before he would proceed; he would not proceed with the work until he had this settlement made. This House approved that two years in succession and voted the money to go on with this tower. Had this settlement been accomplished a year ago, the tower would have been at least partially completed now, because parliament told the minister to go on and complete it. The settlements were made -and this is the point I want to bring out- with the contractor and the architect on the distinct understanding that the completion of the tower was to proceed. After the settlement has been made on that understanding, is it just what one would like to approve, for parliament to come along and say: "We have the settlement out of you; now we are not going to carry out our part and complete that tower?" It is, of course, an embarrassing position for the minister, but not nearly so embarrassing for him as for parliament, not to keep its share of an implied contract with both the contractor and the architect. Those are the plain facts of business. There is not a man in this House who would do such a

thing in his own business. If he had given a contractor a contract for the construction of a residence and had an architect, and had made an agreement with the contractor and the architect to settle differences on the understanding that they would go on and complete the residence, there is not in this House a man who would say then: "Now I have this settlement; I am not going to build the house now; take away your plant."

Does the minister realise that this information was not given to the House before? I think it is unfortunate that the minister did not give us before the information that the settlement with the contractor and the architect was made on the basis that the work was to proceed.

-but I venture to say-and I am prepared to test the feeling of the House upon the question-that the
people of the countiy will not approve of the action of this government in trying to economise on that particular item merely because it is not absolutely necessary to the completion of the tower.

I was one of those who opposed the vote this afternoon, and I said then that what presented the greatest difficulty to me in opposing it was what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) had said. I think the Prime Minister is appealing to the House on entirely wrong grounds at this moment. Personally, I do not know where he gathered the impression that any member in this House was opposed to a memorial chamber. I think the suggestion is absolutely misleading to the country that any member in this House objects to having a memorial chamber in the tower.
That is the very matter provided for in this item.

I stated this afternoon that I wanted to see the tower completed with a memorial chamber; and I am quite satisfied that there is not a member in this House who does not want to see the work done. But what we do suggest is that the tower can be completed and the memorial chamber built in it later on under the plans which now exist.
It is there now, unfinished.

We all hope that this particular architect will be spared to carry out these plans, but if he is not, there will be other architects available, and we can follow the plans some time in the future when we can afford to have the work completed. Let me repeat that the people of Canada expect us to retrench and do away with capital expenditures where possible, for the present, until the country can afford it. We will readily vote the money that is necessary for the tower when the country is able.

I might point out to the Prime Minister that the memorial chamber is already constructed in the tower, with the exception, of course, that the interior is not finished. The very argument I made a moment ago will apply equally well to the memorial chamber: I do not think it would be advisable to finish that chamber until the upper structure of the tower is completed, and that is not likely to be done within the coming fiscal year. Now, there are included in this vote items for extra finishing which is unnecessary and which, as I have pointed

out, cannot possibly be installed this year. That being the case, why include that work now? If it is necessary to do certain work in order to save $80,000 in equipment-and I think there is an argument there that might be considered-if it is absolutely essential, in order to save that money, to go on with the masonry work, to which alone this equipment applies, then perhaps it might be desirable to do so. I should like to get the information definitely from the minister, because I do not think that the committee fully understands the situation, and certainly I do not. The masonry costs $293,000.
I understood the minister to say a while ago $383,000.
I gave the figures for electrical equipment, masonry and so forth, but the masonry is $293,808.
The minister must have misunderstood the question. The masonry work will cost $293,000 or possibly $300,000. Does that include the finishing of the memorial chamber?
No.

It does not include the
finishing of the memorial chamber?
No.

But it includes the completion of the masonry work of the tower. The suggestion I made a moment ago to reduce the vote by $200,000 is very well within the mark. By so doing we would demonstrate to the country that we are quite sincere in paring public expenditures to the utmost.
It seems to me that the minister and the government do not at all realize the situation which tens of thousands of our people are in at the present time.

It would give some of
them work.

I quite recognize
that resuming construction on the tower will give a certain amount of work to a few people here. I also recognize the fact that under a decent system of finance and a proper system of taxation we would have enough money to go ahead with this and a great many other expenditures. But we are dealing with the present financial system, under which, it seems, the government finds it necessary to cut down the most essential 
expenditures. We have had a substantial cut of the grant for agricultural education and of expenditures respecting public health. We must not forget that a great many people throughout the Dominion are struggling to hang on a bit longer while thousands are migrating to the United States to earn a living. I think of many agricultural communities to which I go where there are no proper roads, where men and women are living far from the ordinary social opportunities which they and their families ought to have; I think of hundreds of closed schools on the prairies where another generation is growing up without a chance of even learning to read and write; I think of men and women in my own city of Winnipeg who, not having the ordinary opportunities of acquiring a living, are pinching and scraping to exist,-and I know that this $600,000 must come out of the pockets of the ordinary people. There is no question but that we all feel the need for maintaining the dignity of Canada; there is no doubt wThatever that we would all be pleased to have tourists look up with admiration at a completed tower; and I think there is no hon. member but values fully the aesthetic side of things. But until the government can see its way to make a great many other expenditures and to lighten the load which the people now have to carry, I cannot see that we are justified in voting for such an item as this,

Mr. Chairman,
the discussion has been fairly prolonged, and I think by this time members ought to realize what I have tried to make plain, that the government did not initiate this expenditure. There have been suggestions that this is a political item. That is not true. He represented to the Department of Public Works and to myself as minister that this was a necessary and proper work, and so far as I am concerned the amount was placed in the estimates on his assurance to that effect.

What is the population
of Belle River?

It is a prosperous village on the Grand Trunk railway, an important point on the Canadian side of the lake, seventeen miles east of Windsor. It is at present a harbour of refuge only for shallow draft vessels and gasoline launches, but it is expected that water borne traffic will develop to a considerable extent on the completion of the pier. The population is 008.
Was the contract by tender?
Yes.

What is the tonnage that
it is anticipated will go over this pier?

Mr. Chairman, may I be
permitted to give the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) some information- he seems to be in need of it-with regard to this work? The work is not a dock, it is not a wharf, but it is a breakwater, to protect the entrance to the harbour of Belle River, on which previous governments have spent $28,000. The hon. member asks what connection this has with rum running. Let me tell him that 'the people of my constituency are not quite so familiar with rum running as those of New Brunswick, the province that he represents. There has been a great deal of misrepresentation with regard to this vote, and that misrepresentation has been carried up and down the highways and byways of this country since last year. Last

Supply-Public Works
year I came into this House a new member and I was warned that the leader of the opposition had something on me that would put me out of public life. I was at a loss to know what it was, but when the vote for Belle River came up last year I was almost terrified by the accusations that fell from his bps. Let me say now, as I said then, that never before that afternoon, and never since, except in the possession of the right hon.' leader of the opposition and of a former Minister of Finance of this country, did I see the pamphlet that had been laid at my door. Upon my return to my constituency last year I inquired thoroughly as to where it came from, and not a member of my executive had seen it; not a member of the Conservative executive in the north riding of Essex will say to-night that I have any knowledge of it. The leader of the opposition is about to pay another visit to the constituency that I have the honour to represent. X will leave it to him to ask his own agents there whether or not I am telling the truth. Now, it is easy to attempt to ruin the reputation of a public man by muck-raking. The pamphlet that was held up with such unholy glee by the leader of the opposition and a former Minister of Finance last year has been made the subject of reference' all over the country. The right hon. gentleman carried it from Halifax to British Columbia - and after all what was it? A question of a vote for $30,000 to take care of a harbour that had been recognized by every government for twenty years. On the recommendation of the former Conservative member of the constituency, a customs officer was appointed there. Belle River has a population of some eight hundred French Canadians Last year, out of $2,900,000 ap-9 p.m. preprinted for Ontario, there was only one little vote of $30,000 for [DOT]he French-Canadian population of Belle River, and that was the only vote that the leader of the opposition had the nerve to attack out of that amount of $2,900,000. Well, he has been accused of preaching the doctrine of hate up and down this country; if I had one or two of his speeches here- which I have not, because I did not know this vote was coming on-I would be glad to read from them. But in my constituency actions speak louder than words. As the hon. minister has said, I did not initiate that poor little vote of $30,000, but I was proud to support it, and I made the statement at Belle River and in the city of Windsor, a statement which I am prepared to make tonight, that any vote that was initiated by the former Minister of Railways, whom we

were proud to honour in my constituency and whom this House was proud to honour, is good enough for me to support either in my constituency or in this House.

The hon. member for North Essex (Mr. Healy) has treated us to quite a disquisition. He seemed to come loaded this session and bound to attack me whether I said anything or not. I do not think I have referred to this miserable transaction more than a couple of times since last session, but I want to say to him that its aroma has not been the least improved by the experience meanwhile,- and is not a whit better in point of morals or in point of business since it was initiated last session. The government, as the hon. member, tried to hide behind the skirts of the late lamented Minister of Railways; they said he initiated this vote. Well, it took a long while to appear after the initiation. It was not in the Main Estimates last year; it awaited the result of the election in North Essex, then on the hon. member appearing it came, toward the end of the session, in the Supple-mentaries. I, of course, can say nothing as to what the Minister of Railways did. There is always great pressure on a member to press for anything and everything in his constituency, and possibly the minister yielded; I know nothing of that. But I know from a visit to the riding and I know from correspondence since, that this vote is ' nothing more or less than an outrage, a r6b-bery of the treasury of Canada; that there is no business in Belle River, it does not matter who inhabits the place. There is no business for the breakwater, or the dock or the wharf, or whatever it is. It is simply a waste of the money of Canada, as a reward-

When the vote was up last
year did the right hon. gentleman not admit that some dredging was required in this very harbour?

I do not recall admitting anything of the sort, but I know there is no business there. It may be a place used by gasoline launches-what was it the minister said-as a harbour of refuge? There may possibly be the like of that, but there is no need in the world for a dock or a wharf or a breakwater, and the people of Belle River know it as well as the people of the rest of the riding. Yes, I am going up there, and when I reach Windsor I will express myself as I express myself here in the House of Commons to-night. A pamphlet was published- who published it I think the hon. member

knows as well as I, and who got it printed and circulated. Everybody knows it was printed, and circulated, whoever did it, to help elect the hon. member himself. This was promised; other things were promised, and illegally the pamphlet was scattered through Windsor

several have reached me since. I do not suppose it would be put at the door of the hon. member; he would likely vote right without it, but it was scattered in those quarters where it would be likely to affect the vote, by reason of this promise, by reason of this bribe, and by reason of others that were embraced within it. The government is carrying it out, and on the government's head is the responsibility.

There seems to be an impression that this is a new work. Now, for many years the government have been spending money at Belle River. The engineers have suggested that by building these retaining walls it would be possible to prevent the sedimentation that has been taking place and the necessity for the continued dredging that has hitherto been required. That is, by building this retaining wall iand confining the waters within a certain area the debris will be flushed out, and we will not be called upon each and every year to do this dredging. There is nothing new in this proposition. It is recommended by the engineering department as a proper expenditure, and it is hoped that by constructing these retaining walls we will be able to save money in the end. Representations on the subject have been made by various people. Take the Northern Navigation Company. They represent that this construction, and the deepening of the channel, will permit their boats to ply into that harbour. The item is not a new one. It is one that has come properly before the government, and received proper consideration after being reported on by the engineering department. A vote was properly placed in the estimates last year, the contract has been properly let, and we are now only asking for a revote.
Will the minister tell us what depth of water there is at Belle River?
We hope to secure a depth of ten feet.

Would the minister
tell us how much money has been spent to date at Belle River?
The sum of $28,211 has been spent to date.

In what period, since when?
37i

I have not the date.

I should like to suggest to the-minister that the $28,000, in round figures, of expenditure is since confederation, and represents practically nothing. Now the minister has intimated that this $30,000 is for certain revetment work, and he hopes to get a depth of ten feet. A moment ago he said the depth was not ten feet, so we presume there will be another vote for dredging. What I should like to ask the minister is this: In view of this expenditure, and the peculiar manner in which it was launched-and by the way I noticed the minister rather offered an apology-

No apology at all,
I am only stating facts.
Who are the Northern Navigation Company, where do they ply their steamship line?
They operate between Windsor, Detroit, Michigan and Chatham, Ontario.

Have they got any boats that can be sailed in ten feet of water?
Mr! HEALY: They have-
I was asking the minister.
And I am giving the information.

Here is what the company say in one of their communications:
Our company, who operate a steamer line between Windsor, Ont. Detroit, Michigan and Chatham, Ont. will take advantage of the opportunity which the building of this pier and the dredging of an entrance thereto gives us, by having our steamer use same daily on the vessel's trip, and we believe that the opening of this harbour will materially add to the convenience of the people in the neighbourhood besides very much increasing the value of the property, inasmuch as a large picnic park would be built at this location and there would be thousands of people carried there that formerly did not have the opportunity of visiting the locality.
The manager of the Northern Navigation Company says:
I have personally inspected the location and feel that if the harbour is to be made permanently useful another pier on the west side of the river should be built so as to prevent the bank from falling into the dredged channel, and we hope that the work will be fully completed by the first of June next.
Engineer Craig says:
I am recommending for next year the provision of a sufficient amount to. build a similar extension on the west side of entrance channel and to dredge a channel to a depth of ten feet between the two walls on their completion.

I want to make a statement, now we are at the beginning of a consideration of the estimates. I sit here, in company with a great many other members, and we hear a wrangle when a vote comes up, the leader of the opposition making the statement that the appropriation is of no use, that it is simply a sop to the electors, and a member for the constituency telling us that it is an absolute necessity. Most of us here do not know anything about it. Now, what sort of position is it where two reputable members of the House make statements that are diametrically opposed to each other?
May I point out that one member knows what he is talking about.

The trouble is we are not very sure of* it yet. The statement I want to make, and I want to make it to the government, is this:	That henceforth we shall
require some fair warning of what estimates are going to come up before the House, so that we may have proper time to make an investigation and obtain the necessary information on which to base intelligent criticism of the different items. We go back to our constituents and we are asked about these items, and all the information we have is what is brought out by the stock questions that are put from year to year. That was the case in almost every item that came up last year; there were a few stock questions put that did not amount to anything. What I want is that the government should give fair warning before estimates are brought up for consideration, the night before if they possibly can, so that we may have some opportunity during the next forenoon to make inquiries regarding the nature of the estimate that is to be passed. I want to make a protest against this method of putting estimates through when we have no knowledge whatever of what they really mean.
I want to say to my hon. friend that there is no intention at all on the part of the government-

Excuse me, I do not want to make any insinuations against the government. I offer this suggestion because I believe it to be a good one.
Mr. MACKENZIE KINjp: I was just going to say to my hon. friend that I do not think there has ever been an occasion that notice has not been given the night before of the estimates to be taken up next day. To-day it so happened that there was an understanding 
last night that one of the items in the Public Works department would be proceeded with. I asked the leader of the opposition this afternoon in the presence of the House, whether there would be any objection to going on with the estimates inasmuch as that notice had not been given. Any member, I think, might have objected at the moment,but the House being consulted in the matter did not object and we proceeded. Let me say that if there is the least objection at the moment to going on with these estimates I will ask to have them discontinued. The government has no desire to press the matter. This particular item was discussed last year, and a sum was voted, and all we are asking the House to-night is to revote the amount that parliament then considered and approved of and that was not used. Let me repeat, if any hon. member of the House does not wish to have a discussion of these estimates at the moment I would ask the minister concerned to move that the committee do rise and report progress.

I should like to make the suggestion to the leader of the Progressive group (Mr. Forke), that if there is a conflict of opinion or statement about this wharf or breakwater he should select one of his members to go up and look at the work at Belle River. In the meantime the item could stand, and before it is again considered he could have a report from the member in question as to the character of the place, and the amount of the traffic or tonnage that enters it.
I would be glad to take the hon. member up myself.
I should like to ask the minister if he has any record as to the kind of tonnage that goes in and out of Belle River? How many gasoline launches, and how many steamboats, go in?
May I be permitted to make a statement?
Certainly.

The hon. member (Mr. Hocken) chooses to be a little facetious this evening. If he wants to know anything about Belle River I would be very glad, as I said before, to accompany him there, show him the work, and satisfy him that it is absolutely necessary. As to the tonnage, the Northern Navigation Company is identified with the Canada Steamships Company, that runs large freighters from Sarnia up the lakes. They

also run a line of boats from Detroit to Chatham, drawing ten feet. They have offered to carry passengers daily from Detroit to Belle River and establish a park there just as they have done in other places. The tonnage that has been going in and out of Belle River for the past ten years-and that is the period the $27,000 covers-has been sugar beets from that district to Wallaceburg; and up to the time the channel closed up two years ago, gravel has been carried to build a highway in that district. I make the statement without fear of contradiction, that had that channel been open three years ago, on the gravel used for highways in that district, provincial and county highways, they would have saved $1.50 a yard in freight Under the contract between the Dominion government and the provincial government the local municipalities all get a preference rate on the delivery of gravel. The contract is on file. The local points, such as Belle River, Dresden, Chatham and different points along the river taking advantage of this contract of the provincial government with the Dominion government, are able to buy their gravel and have it delivered at a dollar and a half a yard cheaper than it could be done elsewhere. Had the work been done when it should have been done, as far back as 1919 or 1920, the whole cost of $60,000 which is proposed would have been saved in the past four years to the people of that locality, and now it may eventually cost another $30,000 to protect it on both sides. The engineer is satisfied to try it on one side first. That is a definite statement of fact which is absolutely true.
The right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), has seen fit on several occasions to twit me on the size of the majority that was given me in my election. It was only a little over a thousand, I admit, but I want to point out that in the whole history of that constituency there was only one larger majority given, and that was given to the late Minister of Railways; and we did not call it an election, we called it a landslide, because the people of that locality had decided to give the late Minister of Railways the election by acclamation, but at the last moment the hon. leader of the opposition insisted on election and handpicked a candidate. The gentleman was the handpicked candidate of the right hon. leader of the opposition, and he lost his deposit because half the Conservatives resented the tactics
adopted, and voted for the late Minister of Railways. [DOT] The leader of the opposition speaks of reducing the majority from 7,000 to 1,000. Outside of that one election no candidate in the riding of North Essex received as large a majority as the one given me in my election.
What about the breakwater? That is what we want to hear about.

This is the first opportunity that I have had to resent the slurs cast on me by hon. gentlemen. I think I pointed out the need of the breakwater. These people are entitled to have that channel kept open just as much as the people in any other locality in this country are entitled to have a channel kept open. They have had it kept open for twenty years. The most of the money has been spent in the last ten or twelve years. This is a business proposition, to get away from the continual annual waste of money by putting this small entrance-that is all it is-to this harbour in a condition so that the government will not be called upon from year to year to spend from two to five to ten thousand dollars for dredging. It is a straight business proposition. The files will show that it was not initiated by myself. But I came here as a representative of the people, and the first opportunity I had to take a hand in the matter was when the Supplementary Estimates came up, and, as representing that locality, I asked the government to include it in the vote. That is a simple statement of the fact. It is a very small vote, but it is just as necessary for these people as the millions voted for the harbour of Toronto are for the people there, and just as important as the millions being asked for by British Columbia and placed in the vote of this year. It is just as important as the amount asked for by Fort William and Port Arthur. These are larger places, but the smaller community has some rights in this country, and I am going to represent the small community just as much as the great city of Windsor, whenever I believe they have rights, and I am not ashamed to stand up and fight for their rights at any time either at home or here.
Can the minister give me the information I ask for? There is a customs officer there and there should be a record.	[DOT]

I have not the
customs returns, but we are advised there is a quantity of sugar beets transported from that point. The sand and gravel business

which has been mentioned is of interest to the municipality; in fact the municipality themselves have recommended that this work shall be done. This work would also permit of their bringing in coal, lumber and building material, and would help in the developing of the fishing industry. I understand the minister cannot give me the information I ask for.
I have not the customs return.
I think it would be interesting to this House if we knew how many gasoline launches or how many boats used those waters.

We have not the
customs returns in regard to the traffic in and out. I do not suppose it can be very big, because I understand the channel is blocked at the present time. It has been closed for two years. It is like many channels that have been allowed to fill up; and I should say, from what I can learn, that it should be opened up, and that these people should have access to the water to carry on their business.
I would not exclude them by any means because of the fact that they are a small community. Parliament authorized an expenditure of $30,000 last year and a contract has been entered into. It is a revote.

Do I understand that
there has been no traffic there at all? Why not let the item stand until we get the customs return?-because we ought to have this information.

I think we ought to have some description of this place. Has there been dredging done in the past?
Mr, KING (Kootenay):	No.

What is the depth of water
at the present time, and how far out from the shore do you have to go to get the necessary depth of water? From what I have heard it appears to me a channel will have to be dug, and there is a bay inside, or something of that kind. I think we should have some proper description of the locality, and let us understand what it is. Is it simply an effort being made to make a harbour, or is there to some extent a natural harbour there which merely requires improvement?
Is this place on the shore of lake St. Clair?
Yes.

From the little I know of that locality, it is very shallow and you would have to go out a very long way to get ten feet of water. Can the minister tell me what number of feet the largest boat ever entering up to date would draw? Would it be anything like ten feet, or would it be three or four feet? If I know anything about it, I imagine you would have to. go out six or seven hundred feet to get five feet of water. If this is an effort to make a harbour at a place where there is not a natural harbour, there is nothing to warrant it. I live on the shores of lake Simcoe and I could name any number of municipalities where they would be only too glad to get an appropriation for a breakwater, where they have a great depth of water. But that is no reason for such construction. If the department would listen to all the municipalities who would like to have something of this nature done, we could smother them with requests. The point is, is this needed? Is there any traffic there? Are there any boats of any size which come in and out, or is it merely a question of some pleasure launches that are used there for amusement? If the minister cannot furnish me with that information, perhaps the hon. member for North Essex (Mr. Healy) would be able to do so.

We are desirous
of giving all information possible regarding this or any other item. This is an old harbour that has been used for many years. During the war, I think there was not much doing, and the harbour was allowed to silt up. Boats have been using the harbour from time to time, and suggestions have been made that it should be opened up again for the advantage of the people there. I would be glad to get for my hon. friend further information in regard to the customs returns and any other information desired. I would say: Let the item stand for the present until we get that information. There is no hurry.
The next item is Blind river, wharf construction, $10,000. I would move that that be struck out. I am advised that the contract will be completed and the money paid from this year's appropriation. It is not necessary to revote it.

about the item under consideration? We agreed to take the items seriatim.

Blind river in?

I know a number of members have been taken by surprise in the matter, and more progress would be made if, after investigation, these matters were taken up.

subtopic: EQUALITY OP GROUNDS FOR RELIEF AS BETWEEN THE SEXES

speechtext:
The House resumed from Wednesday, March 19, the debate on the motion of Mr.' Shaw:
That, in the opinion of this House, legislation should be introduced in order to place the wife on an equality with the husband as regards the grounds upon which divorce may be obtained.
Mr. WILLIAM IRVINE (East Calgary: The resolution is so reasonable that I think the House should pass it without very much more discussion. I was very much surprised the other day to find that a considerable number of hon. gentlemen objected to it on the ground that divorce would be much more easily obtainable if the resolution were passed and legislation were introduced in harmony with it. Those who listened to the argument as advanced by the mover of the resolution (Mr. Shaw) will be convinced, I think, that there is no reason for anxiety in that regard.
All that is asked is simply that women be placed exactly on an equality with men with respect to the granting of divorces. There seems to be no real room for argument against the motion. There is one point I wish to mention. In this regard the province

of Alberta, and I think the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan as well, are in a position of considerable difficulty; they have not the same rights as the provinces of Quebec amd Ontario. I do hope that the House will pass the resolution without further discussion.
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Ministe^ of Railways and Canals): When this matter was last under consideration some fear was expressed that if it were introduced in the form of a bill and put among the public bills and orders it might not be reached. But in order that there might be an opportunity for full discussion I suggested-and I think the suggestion was accepted-that. the resolution be dropped on the assurance of the government that if a bill were introduced it would be reached in due course.
Mr. JOS. T. SHAW (West Calgary): The arrangement which I had with the Minister of Railways was substantially as has just been stated by him. We both contemplated that the resolution would not be reached, and in view of the fact that some suggestion had been made that the matter should be put in the form of a public bill and so introduced,
I then proposed to the minister that if he would give me an assurance that it would receive consideration in that form, despite the fact that it woud be among Public Bills and Orders, I would have no objection to presenting it as a bill. In view of the fact that the minister gives such an assurance I have no objection to withdrawing the resolution. I want it understood, however, that the motion is withdrawn on the understanding that when the bill which I shall introduce comes up for second reading I shall have an opportunity, before the end of the session, of pressing that reading.
Resolution withdrawn.
